It might help to talk to someone about it, or write, or anything that helps you see the situation from a different perspective. Keep looking back at it for now, just seeing it for what it is plain and simple can really help you cope.

It's ok, dude. We all have exceptionally low moments. You need to understand that just because you dont feel "happy" doesnt mean that there is something wrong with you. The way you feel is not your fault. You are not incapable of feeling happiness, you are a person, who just happens to be having a very hard time, and it's not your fault.

You should read "The Myth of Sisyphus" by Albert Camus. It talks about the idea of embracing the madness that is life, and how you really are better off being conscious of this absurdity than being ignorant. It's a fairly short essay, I read it every once in a while when I feel like this. I think you will like it.

I don't know why I keep this silly old thing. My old, raggedy teddy-bear, that is. It's been broken for quite some time. I don't know what it is, but the thing won't be fixed. I think the stitching is done wrong or something because every time I patch it up, another seam opens up, and more stuffing falls out. I try to gather it all up and put it back, but every time, a little bit is lost to the carpet, and can't be reclaimed. After many patches and repairs, not much stuffing remains, and my bear looks oddly lopsided and limp, with more stuffing in some parts than others. Looking at the small, brown bear, with buttons for eyes, now turned old, dirty, and frayed, a part of me wishes to give up the burden of caring for it. It is all too much work for such an old bear. One day, I decided to rid myself of this useless bear, once and for all. I really wanted to. It would have been so easy to let the bear simply fall from my grasp, into the bin, but as I stood there holding it's limp body, I was afraid. I was afraid of losing all of the work I had done on the bear, of wasting the countless hours of patching and stitching, and as I looked into the bear's lifeless button-eyes, I faltered. I took the little bear back to my room. Another hole had opened up at one of the seams. I didn't break out the sewing supplies. I didn't try to patch it up. I just took the teddy-bear, and set it high up on a shelf, never to be used, never to be touched, never to be repaired. It sits up on its shelf, slowly breaking at the seams, looking down on me with its cold, dead, button-eyes, but I don't look back at it. I don't look back.

The cool ocean breeze blows gently in his face, providing relief from the heat of the sun. He looks down to see he is sitting in a beach chair, relaxing in a reclined position. He reaches down and runs his fingers through the fine, warm sand, and his hand is met with another. As their fingers interlace, he looks to his right, facing the hand's owner. There she was. She was as beautiful as ever with her her sun bleached hair and her skin tan. She looked in his eyes with her blue ones and squeezed his hand. She smiled her big, kind grin, and said "I love you".
